summary: Specifies the MPLS base YANG data model, a framework for configuring and managing the MPLS switching function on a router. Other MPLS-related YANG models, such as those for static LSPs, LDP, or RSVP-TE, are expected to build on it.

eli5.summary: A standard settings form for the part of a router that forwards packets by labels, so management tools from different makers can all fill it in.

subtitle: A standard YANG model that lets management tools configure and read the MPLS forwarding function of a router.

tldr.problem: Operators need one common, machine-readable way to configure and inspect the MPLS switching function on routers from different makers, and later MPLS features need a shared base to build on.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8960 defines the ietf-mpls YANG module. It adds MPLS data to the generic routing RIB model from RFC 8349, creates a native MPLS RIB instance, and defines label blocks, MPLS-enabled interfaces and next hop label forwarding entries.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and a base framework: other MPLS YANG modules, such as static LSP, LDP or RSVP-TE models, are expected to augment it.

today: RFC 8960 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself expects other modules, such as MPLS static LSP, LDP or RSVP-TE models, to augment it.

sections.title: Why an MPLS Base Model
sections.content:
A core routing YANG model already exists in RFC 8349. It describes a generic Routing Information Base (RIB) that does not depend on the address family, plus instances for IPv4 and IPv6. RFC 8960 adds the MPLS part, following the MPLS architecture of RFC 3031.

Its stated purpose is to supply essential building blocks. It is meant as a base for future YANG modules covering more sophisticated MPLS features and for different control-plane protocols. The text expects other IETF modules, for example from the TEAS and MPLS Working Groups, to augment it. The module conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342.
sections.eli5: There is already a standard form for a router's routing table. This document adds the extra boxes needed for label-based forwarding, so later documents can keep adding to the same form.

sections.title: Two Ways the Model Touches the RIB
sections.content:
The model works in two ways. First, it augments existing address-family RIBs. An IPv4 prefix in the IPv4 RIB, for example, can carry an MPLS local label and one or more per-next-hop remote labels, which enables MPLS forwarding for that prefix.

Second, it creates a new RIB instance for native MPLS routes, by extending the address-family identity from RFC 8349 with a new mpls identity. These are routes that are enabled for MPLS forwarding but are not stored in another address-family RIB.

The RFC gives these examples of native MPLS routes:

  • Routes programmed by RSVP on the Label Switching Routers along an LSP.
  • Routes that cross-connect a local label to a Layer 2 or Layer 3 VRF.
  • Routes that cross-connect a local label to a Layer 2 adjacency such as an Attachment Circuit.
  • Routes that cross-connect a local label to a Layer 3 adjacency such as a Segment Routing Adjacency Segment or Binding SID (RFC 8402).
sections.eli5: The router already keeps a list of where to send packets. The model lets each entry also carry a sticker label, and it adds a separate list just for destinations that exist only as labels.

sections.title: Building Blocks of the ietf-mpls Module
sections.content:
The module defines two identities. mpls represents the native MPLS RIB, and label-block-alloc-mode is a base for label-block allocation modes. The module itself derives mpls-unicast from mpls, and two allocation modes: one where the label manager handles allocation within the reserved block, and one where the application does.

Two enumerations are defined. mpls-operations-type lists the operations impose-and-forward, pop-and-forward, pop-impose-and-forward, swap-and-forward and pop-and-lookup. nhlfe-role says whether a next hop is primary, backup or primary-and-backup.

The core data structure is the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE), used when forwarding a labeled packet. It holds the packet's next hop and the operation to perform on the label stack: replace the top label, pop, replace and then push more labels, or push labels onto an unlabeled packet. It may also hold the data-link encapsulation, the way to encode the label stack and any other information needed to dispose of the packet. A single-next-hop grouping and a multiple-next-hop grouping are provided.

For multiple next hops, each entry has an index, a backup-index that refers to a backup entry (see RFC 4090 and RFC 5714), a loadshare value defaulting to 1 for unequal load balancing, and a role. A share is the ratio of an entry's number to the total across all next hops.
sections.eli5: Each label entry is like a to-do card for the router: where to send the packet next, and what to do with its stack of stickers. Cards can also say who is the main route and who is the spare, and how to split traffic.

sections.title: Global, Interface and Label-Block Data
sections.content:
The module adds an mpls container under /routing. It is meant as the attachment point for other MPLS sub-features, such as static LSPs, LDP LSPs and Traffic Engineering LSP tunnels. It holds three things.

  • ttl-propagate, a boolean that defaults to true, controls propagating TTL between IP and MPLS.
  • mpls-label-blocks is a list keyed by index, with a start-label, an end-label, a block-allocation-mode and a read-only inuse-labels-count. A must rule requires the start label to be less than or equal to the end label.
  • interfaces lists interfaces by name, with a mpls-enabled flag that defaults to false and a maximum-labeled-packet size in octets (see RFC 3032).

On routes, the module adds mpls-enabled (default false) and mpls-local-label, which applies only when MPLS is enabled for the route. For native MPLS RIB routes it also adds destination-prefix and route-context. The label stack entries carry a label, a TTL and a traffic class. The active-route action is augmented as well, so a query can be made by MPLS local label on the native MPLS RIB.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of switches on the form: one master setting about countdown timers, a list of label ranges the router may hand out, and a list saying which network ports speak labels.

sections.title: The Example Data Tree
sections.content:
Appendix A shows an example instance of the data tree in JSON, following RFC 7951. A router R1 has IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes with MPLS labels 16001 to 16004, two interfaces named eth0 and eth1, and an RSVP LSP tunnel with Tunnel-ID 10 and LSP-ID 1.

In the IPv4 RIB, a route for 198.51.100.1/32 is shown with mpls-enabled set to true, a local label of 16001 and a label stack entry with TTL 255. The example illustrates how ordinary IP routes are decorated with MPLS data rather than duplicated.
sections.eli5: The appendix is a worked example: a sample router with a few labeled destinations, shown the way a management tool would see them.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement transports are SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict who may do what.

The RFC calls out the writable start-label and end-label nodes under the label blocks: writing to them may disrupt existing traffic. Reading the augmented next-hop data, and using the active-route action, may disclose next-hop and per-prefix route information that could be used for further attacks. The security considerations of RFC 3031 and RFC 3032 also apply.

For IANA, the document registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-mpls and the YANG module ietf-mpls with prefix mpls.
sections.eli5: Because the form controls how a router sends traffic, only trusted people should be able to edit it, and even reading it could show an attacker the routes.
